title: Google Antigravity launches Mass Spec Skills, lifting molecular identification accuracy from under 4% to about 97%
summary: Anyone who works with mass spectra knows the bottleneck: instruments detect abundant molecular signals, but routine spectral library searches annotate only about 5% on average. Google DeepMind has added a set of Mass Spec Skills to Antigravity, letting the AI agent call established chemistry tools and query public databases to turn spectra directly into molecular structures.
ai_summary: Google DeepMind has released Mass Spec Skills for Antigravity: the AI agent can now run established mass-spec tools and query public chemical libraries to interpret spectra as molecular structures. Routine library search annotates about 5% of spectra on average, and about 10% for human samples. On a benchmark of 100 compounds with public library references, models without internet or skills scored under 4%; with the skills, all three models identified and verified the correct molecule in about 97% of attempts, with the lightweight model matching the frontier models. The skills also sharply cut generated tokens per attempt: by nearly 4x on the lightweight model, and by half and nearly a fifth on the two frontier models. They are most useful for metabolomics, natural products and drug discovery researchers. Limits: mirror-image molecules, closely related isomers and molecules absent from databases still cannot be confirmed by spectrum alone.
brief: Routine spectral library searches annotate only about 5% of measured spectra on average, and about 10% for human samples; the rest is the "dark matter" of mass spectrometry.
In one end-to-end example, 19 useful peaks were extracted from 1,761 raw peaks; the correct structure was pinned down among 845 PubChem isomers and accounted for 97.7% of fragment intensity.
On a 100-compound benchmark, accuracy was under 4% without the skills and about 97% with them, with the lightweight model matching frontier models.
DeepMind is offering 10,000 scientists free access to Antigravity's highest usage tier for 6 months, onboarded on a rolling basis.

sections.h: What it is: a one-sentence background

blocks.p: Mass Spec Skills is a suite of domain skills inside Google Antigravity. Antigravity is Google's AI agent product -- think of it as an assistant that can call tools on its own. The skills are a professional toolkit bolted onto it: they let it run established mass-spec software, query public chemical databases for you, and combine the results into a reviewable conclusion using Gemini's reasoning.
In short, what an analytical chemist once did manually step by step can now be described in natural language; the agent chooses the skills, chains the workflow, and produces a report.

sections.h: Why mass spectra are so hard to identify: libraries cover only 5%

blocks.p: Blood, soil and plant tissue are full of small molecules: nutrients, hormones, drugs and their metabolites, pollutants, and bioactive compounds with potential therapeutic value. A modern mass spectrometer can detect tens of thousands of molecular signals from a single drop of sample extract. Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), which first breaks molecules apart and then measures the fragments, can also show what they split into.

Detecting a signal is not the same as knowing which molecule made it. The standard approach is to match each spectrum against reference spectra of known molecules. The problem: even after a decade of library expansion, only about 5% of measured spectra are annotated on average, and about 10% for human samples. The rest is known in the field as the "dark matter" of mass spectrometry.

callout.title: How to think about an MS/MS spectrum
callout.text: It is like knowing the parts list of a crashed car -- the mass of each fragment -- without knowing what the original car looked like. Library matching is like checking whether an identical car's parts list exists. When there is no match, you have to reconstruct the original structure from the parts.

blocks.p: Many of the unannotated molecules are already listed in public chemical databases; their spectra have just never been recorded, so there is no reference to match. Identifying them requires inferring the structure directly from the fragment ions. Analytical chemists have a mature workflow: search spectral libraries, determine the molecular formula, pull candidate structures from a database, and test each candidate against the observed fragment peaks. The tools are already available and open source, but every spectrum still takes an expert considerable time -- and a single study can produce large numbers of spectra, which manual analysis simply cannot keep up with.

sections.h: A full example: from 1,761 peaks to one structure

blocks.p: DeepMind used a negative-ion spectrum -- traditionally harder to annotate than positive ion -- to demonstrate the end-to-end workflow. The raw spectrum contained 1,761 peaks. First, matchms removed more than 1,700 low-intensity noise spikes, leaving 19 useful fragment peaks.

Next, SIRIUS determined the molecular formula C20H21ClN6O with a mass error of -1.5 ppm and a score of 37.86, well ahead of the runner-up at 28.33. Once the formula is fixed, the agent can search a database for candidates with the same formula.

The agent retrieved and scored all 845 same-formula isomers from PubChem. Several top candidates each accounted for 14 of the 19 peaks and 97.7% of summed fragment intensity -- by mass match alone, they were nearly indistinguishable.

At that point, chemistry reasoning takes over. The observed neutral losses point to a central urea linkage: it loses HCl, then isocyanic acid HNCO, and can also form the same loop in the opposite order. Isomers without a urea linkage were ruled out. The urea bond cleaves into two complementary halves with 45.1% and 6.8% of fragment intensity; their formulas add up exactly to the intact parent.

To separate the two most similar candidates, the agent also looked at the bond-breakage penalty: the correct structure's cumulative bond-break score was 26.0 versus 49.0 for the runner-up, with lower meaning less costly. Finally, RDKit verified that the winning structure is chemically valid and matches the exact mass; the agent then drew the 2D structure, marked the key cleavage sites and produced a reviewable report.

blocks.p: To test reliability, DeepMind sampled 100 compounds from the Enamine REAL MS/MS collection in MoNA -- structures also catalogued in PubChem -- after removing records that barely fragmented. Each spectrum was attempted three times, and any attempt exceeding a one-hour budget counted as a failure.

Three setups were compared: fully offline with no skills, internet access only, and internet access plus the Mass Spec Skills. With no internet and no skills, all three models scored under 4% -- confirming that they cannot deduce structures from the peak list alone.

With internet access only, the models could query online libraries, but their improvised search scripts proved brittle around precursor windows, adducts and noisy peaks: the frontier models missed a quarter to a third of spectra, and the lightweight model missed more than three-quarters.
After adding Mass Spec Skills, all three models identified and verified the exact molecule in about 97% of attempts, with the lightweight model catching up to the frontier models.

sections.h: Token cost: how the skills save

blocks.p: The skills don't just improve accuracy; they also save money. With no internet or skills, the models burned the most tokens per attempt trying to brute-force structures from raw peak lists. With internet only, they still spent substantial tokens improvising API queries and debugging one-off scripts.

With Mass Spec Skills, Antigravity calls validated, ready-made skills, and generated tokens per attempt dropped across every model: by nearly four times on the lightweight Gemini 3.8 Flash, by half on Gemini 4 Argon, and by nearly a fifth on Gemini 4 Carbon.

blocks.p: Several collaborators shared concrete impressions. Phanankosi Moyo of the University of Pretoria said the skills have the potential to transform natural-product drug discovery, with prediction accuracy above 90% in most of their evaluations, even for highly complex structures.

fig.subtitle: This is the collaborator's own evaluation, not a formal benchmark
fig.text: Their remarkable accuracy in predicting even highly complex molecular structures (>90% in most of our evaluations)

blocks.p: Scott Jarmusch, assistant professor at the Technical University of Denmark, said work that used to take days or months of analysis and literature review can now be done in hours, letting chemists prioritize features in their data faster. Xi Xing of Princeton University described it as a "golden triad": Gemini, the AI agent and the skills together feel like hiring a small team that can compute, look things up and propose ideas.

list: The post doesn't say how many tokens or analyses are included in the free 6 months of the "highest usage tier."
It doesn't explain how the 10,000 free spots are selected or what the acceptance rate is; it only says onboarding is "rolling."
Pricing for the Enterprise plan and individual paid tiers has not been announced.
The post doesn't link to the 100-compound benchmark dataset or say whether it is public and reproducible.
It doesn't list which mass spectrometer vendors' raw data formats are supported.
There is no quantified comparison of time or accuracy against using open-source tools such as SIRIUS or GNPS directly.

blocks.p: Start with the value: the skills automate the whole grind of searching libraries, determining formulas, screening candidates and validating structures, while keeping the evidence chain reviewable. For omics researchers drowning in unannotated spectra, the time saved is real.

The tradeoffs: for now this lives inside Antigravity, so you need to download the app and install the plugin; enterprise users log in with Google Cloud credentials, and pricing outside the free tier is unknown. It cannot distinguish mirror-image molecules (chirality) or some closely related isomers, and it cannot confirm genuinely new molecules that aren't in any database.

If you work in metabolomics, environmental samples or natural-product screening and have a pile of unannotated spectra, it's worth applying for the free tier. If you're an analytical chemist or student new to computational tools, it lowers the technical barrier. If you need authoritative, regulated identification or confirmation of a new structure, this gives you a starting point and evidence -- not a final conclusion that replaces orthogonal measurements such as NMR.
